title: How to Do Great Work
note: The reframe away from hustle: problem selection beats execution skill, and morale compounds like interest — extract the part on how curiosity picks the problem for you.

title: How To Be Successful
note: The 90th-vs-99th-percentile divide needs smart AND hard work, and wealth comes from ownership not salary — note that most outliers were contrarian at exactly one moment.

title: Relentlessly Resourceful
note: The surgical resourceful-vs-hapless contrast — read it as a spec for the one response pattern to train in yourself and screen for in cofounders.

title: What I Wish Someone Had Told Me
note: The "inaction is insidious risk" and "hard thing that matters > easy thing that doesn't" lines — use them to re-rank what you actually work on this quarter.

title: Founder Mode
note: The gaslighting-dynamic framing — extract why your resistance to standard delegation advice is detection, not a flaw, before you scale the team.

title: Earnestness
note: The formidable + earnest = unstoppable thesis — take the point that caring about the problem itself is an unfakeable competitive advantage.

title: How to Think for Yourself
note: The Dunning-Kruger inversion (conventional-minded people are most sure they're independent): audit your own contrarianism against the three components here.

title: Advice
note: Operating under uncertainty is a different skill than learning, and peer-group contamination is the silent killer — extract how to manage your input set as you scale.

title: Schlep Blindness
note: The Stripe example in full — the bias that hides the best ideas is psychological aversion to tedious work, and the schlep is the moat.

title: Do Too Much: How to be a leader
note: His one essay on founder mentality: 'you are the upper bound for how much anyone in your company will care; too much is the right amount.' The earnestness principle operationalized at 19, with stakes.

title: Superlinear Returns
note: Returns at the top are exponential plus a threshold, not linear: a product half as good takes none of the market, so the safe, evenly-rewarded path is the wrong one. The practical consequence is to follow curiosity into the questions that mystify you, because that is where the uncrowded, threshold-crossing payoffs sit. A distinct lens from Great Work on why problem-selection itself is where the compounding lives.

title: The Right Kind of Stubborn
note: Persistence and obstinacy look identical from outside and invert on one axis: the persistent person fixes on the goal and stays flexible on means, updating on evidence; the obstinate one fixes on the means and is driven by ego. The self-check when you hit a wall is whether the evidence still supports the goal, or only your pride does.

title: Why Product Sense is the only product skill that will matter in the AI age
note: The five-part model (empathy, simulation, strategy, taste, creative execution) for the judgment AI won't commoditize — your defensible layer.

title: How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product/Market Fit
note: The single-question PMF survey and the four-step loop — copy this directly into Skale to make PMF measurable.

title: Karri Saarinen's 10 Rules for Crafting Products That Stand Out
note: Linear's operating manual: small connected teams, everyone owns quality, opinionated over flexible.

title: Product Strategy Means Saying No
note: The clearest short case that refusal is a product capability and every feature is a permanent liability.

title: Linear's Path to Product-Market Fit
note: Building for a specific someone and refusing flexibility — why opinionated constraints make a product feel inevitable.

title: Know Your Customers' "Jobs to Be Done"
meta: Clayton Christensen et al. · article · medium
note: The milkshake formulation — frame discovery around the functional/social/emotional job, not the feature.

title: Is There Such a Thing as Good Taste?
note: The argument the whole "taste is real, not subjective" claim rests on: good design has properties you can learn to see, shown by reductio.

title: Product vs. Feature Teams
note: The canonical short distinction the whole empowered-team model rests on: give teams problems to solve, not features to build.

title: Opportunity Solution Trees
note: The written reference for the OST framework: map outcome to opportunities to solutions to testable assumptions, to keep discovery aligned with the outcome.

title: How to Hire a Product Manager
note: The founding essay of modern PM hiring, still the most-cited in the field: what separates a real product manager from a project manager with a fancier title.

title: The Power of Product Thinking
note: Product thinking as a trainable skill — knowing what makes a product useful and loved — worked backward from human behavior, with the Facebook Reactions case study.

title: What's Your Shape? A 12-competency model for product leaders
note: The most rigorous public model for diagnosing a product leader's strengths and gaps, and the 'spiky vs round' insight: elite leaders are pointy and hire to cover the rest.

title: How to develop product sense
note: The how-to companion to Shreyas's product-sense essay: four concrete, trainable mechanisms for building product sense, with real YouTube and Slack examples.

title: Malleable Software: Restoring User Agency in a World of Locked-Down Apps
meta: Geoffrey Litt et al. (Ink & Switch) · essay · ~35 min
note: The research lab that actually ships these prototypes arguing the unit to dispense with is 'the application' itself: software you reshape to fit your work, backed by working systems rather than slideware. It reframes what is worth building 18 months out, tools users mold instead of products they consume.

title: Why Chatbots Are Not the Future
note: The affordances argument with live demos: a bare text box signals nothing about what the tool can do and forces constant switching between deciding and evaluating, which kills flow. The canonical statement of the anti-chat case, from someone who builds the interfaces.

title: Squish Meets Structure: Designing with Language Models
note: A design framework, not a chat critique: treat language models as squishy systems and find the Goldilocks zone by constraining them into small, observable reasoning steps instead of one magic box that overpromises. The build-around-probabilism model that most later anti-chatbot takes are downstream of.

title: A Field Guide to Rapidly Improving AI Products
note: From 30+ production builds: the teams that win barely discuss tools and obsess over measurement, you start from bottom-up error analysis not off-the-shelf metrics (one client's core bug was date-handling failing 66% of the time, invisible to generic scores), and the custom data viewer is the highest-leverage thing you build. Distinct from his 'Your AI Product Needs Evals' (why) — this is the operating manual (how).

title: Product Judgment: How some people repeatedly create product success
note: Intercom's CPO on the uncomfortable claim the trainability essays skip: product judgment is domain-specific and does not transfer. He went from YouTube and Gmail to B2B with zero judgment in the new domain and rebuilt it only by talking to 100+ customers for competence and 1,000+ for proficiency (reports and recordings do not count), with a three-rates-of-change model for which judgment ages well.

title: Invisible Details of Interaction Design
note: The named mechanisms (physics, gesture responsiveness, contextual affordances) behind the "magic" feeling — use it as a checklist of decisions you're currently leaving on defaults.

title: Great Animations
note: The six-test filter for motion that earns its place vs motion that's decoration — apply "purpose" and "interruptible" to every Skale animation.

title: Jiro's Dream
note: The ur-argument that taste is a learnable, transferable palate you build by consuming great work — read it once a quarter.

title: How We Redesigned the Linear UI
meta: Karri Saarinen et al. · article · medium
note: The surgical decision log: LCH color migration, 98→3 color variables, Inter Display for hierarchy — a rare live narration of taste trade-offs.

title: Design Engineering at Vercel
note: The definition of design engineering as one discipline (perf + a11y + polish), not a designer-to-engineer handoff — your structural advantage as a solo CTO.

title: Apple Human Interface Guidelines
note: Read it for the perceptual reasoning behind metaphor, feedback, and direct manipulation — not as a checklist, as the "why apps that ignore this feel wrong."

title: Web Interface Guidelines
note: A version-controlled checklist of the implementation-level calls a model leaves on defaults: fade-and-scale dialogs from ~0.8 not 0, press buttons to ~0.96, tabular-nums so timers and number columns do not reflow, 16px input font to stop iOS zoom, pause off-screen loops, no dead zones between list items. The literal operationalization of this section's thesis that great-versus-slop is a thousand small decisions no model makes for you.

title: Do Things That Don't Scale
note: The primary-source argument for why your first 100 customers come through you by hand, not through automation or a funnel.

title: Finding Language/Market Fit
note: Use ad-copy tests to find the exact words that make X founders feel read before you touch the product.

title: How to Win Your First 10 B2B Customers
note: Follow the channel sequence (network → cold outbound → investors' networks → communities) synthesized from 20+ founders including Vanta and Figma.

title: How Today's Fastest Growing B2B Businesses Found Their First Ten Customers
note: Read the primary first-customer tactics from Stripe, Slack, and Plaid alongside the newer version for the full pattern.

title: The SaaS Org Chart
note: Use the seed→A→B hiring map to avoid hiring a VP of Sales before you personally have a repeatable close.

title: Growth+Sales: The New Era of Enterprise Go-to-Market
meta: Peter Lauten & Martin Casado (a16z) · essay · ~20 min
note: Consciously pick or reject the PLG + top-down dual motion, and learn its six failure modes, before Series A.

title: AMA with Steli Efti — Pricing, Selling, and Building Sales Teams
note: Get the practitioner answers on when to start charging, how to write a cold email that gets replies, and when to fire a customer.

title: How I've approached founder-led sales
note: The granular call mechanics the funnel-level pieces skip, from Lattice's #3 turned Dock CEO: reframe the early call as a feedback call so the objective is fixing the product, run a 25-minute anatomy (founding story and qualify, demo with question breaks, next steps), close by building the prospect's space from their own collateral, make a pilot the goal, and keep a deliberately minimal CRM so speed beats data hygiene.

title: Five ways to build a $100 million business
note: The five customer animals (elephants, deer, rabbits, mice, flies): your average revenue per account dictates the entire GTM machine, so $100M means either ~1,000 elephants at $100k+ via high-touch sales or ~100,000 rabbits at $1k via self-serve inbound. The upstream decision that determines whether founder-led enterprise sales even applies to you, before any first-call tactic matters.

title: The Cold Start Problem
note: Use the atomic-network → tipping-point → escape-velocity taxonomy to diagnose which stage Skale is actually in, so you stop running wrong-stage tactics.

meta: Brian Balfour, Casey Winters, Kevin Kwok, Andrew Chen · essay · ~20min
note: Re-architect Skale's growth as a self-reinforcing loop so CAC compounds down instead of leaking out of a funnel.

title: How the biggest consumer apps got their first 1,000 users
note: The data that gives you permission to bet everything on one channel: most winners used exactly one.

title: Braindump on Viral Loops
note: The retention-drives-K math that tells you to fix churn before optimizing your viral coefficient.

title: In Consumer AI, Momentum Is the Moat
note: The distribution-velocity-as-moat thesis: whoever runs ship-distribute-iterate fastest pulls away, because feature moats evaporate.

title: Come for the Tool, Stay for the Network
note: The exact sequencing for getting single-player utility to critical mass before the network layer matters.

title: Notes on Superhuman's Acquisition Loops
note: How to design a bragging-rights loop where users proselytize for status, not utility.

title: Growth Hacker is the New VP Marketing
note: The "where do my users already congregate" mental model, via the canonical Airbnb/Craigslist hack.

title: Bootstrapping Side Projects into Profitable Startups
note: The build-in-public + niche-community + product-is-the-marketing playbook from someone who did it solo with zero ad spend.

title: How to Launch a Dev Tool on Hacker News
note: The tactical Show HN playbook for technical products: title framing, timing, and priming engagers without vote-begging.

title: My Solopreneur Story: Zero to $45K/mo
note: The exact "build an X audience first, then launch into a 1,000-person invite gate" loop — your channel, your move.

title: The Stair Step Method of Bootstrapping
note: Start inside an existing ecosystem (app store, plugin directory) for built-in distribution before going standalone.

title: Four Fits For $100M+ Growth
note: The directionality most people get backwards: products are built to fit channels, channels never mold to products, and your revenue model decides which channels are even available before you spend a dollar. The four-fit framework (Market/Product, Product/Channel, Channel/Model, Model/Market) turns 'pick one channel' from a guess into a deductible decision.

title: Invisible Asymptotes
note: Amazon's first strategic-planning analyst on how to find the hidden ceiling every growth curve hits: interrogate the people who do not buy, not your fans. At Amazon the asymptote was shipping-fee hatred, and the fix was Prime. The companion to momentum-as-moat, because it names what kills momentum before the curve flattens.

title: How to Get Rich (without getting lucky)
note: The leverage taxonomy (labor/capital/code/media) that explains why a technical founder with an X audience is a different category of person — map your Rust + multi-agent + SaaS stack directly onto "specific knowledge + code + permissionless media."

title: Most Human Wins
note: The 2025 answer to "everyone has Codex": taste, judgment, and embodied reputation are the moat, not speed of output — read it as your positioning brief for not becoming a wrapper.

title: 1,000 True Fans
note: The proof you need ~1K paying advocates, not mass reach — reframe X from vanity metrics to building the exact 1K who'll pre-buy Lancelot and seed skale-brain.

title: Spiky Point of View: Let's Get a Little Controversial
note: The single tactic that separates compounding founder accounts from stagnant ones — turn your benchmark numbers and architecture opinions into a defensible spiky stance.

title: The Ultimate Guide to Writing Online
note: The Personal Monopoly concept — how "Rust framework + AI agent ops + Central Asian operator" becomes a magnet instead of noise.

title: How Would You Build an Audience from Scratch in 2024?
note: Nine non-obvious lessons from 500K+ followers — the core one: build the magnet for WHO you want, because who follows you beats how many.

title: MAKE: The Indie Maker Blueprint
note: The operational bible for shipping solo with X as the product itself — read the revenue-transparency-as-distribution section first.

title: Don't Call Yourself A Programmer, And Other Career Advice
note: The reframe that you sell outcomes, not skills — the framing discipline to apply to every post about Lancelot and Skale.

title: Reflecting on My Failure to Build a Billion-Dollar Company
note: Proof that radical honesty about real numbers is the highest-signal founder content — the template for your own build-in-public posts.

title: Status as a Service
note: Why X mechanically rewards high-effort technical posting: social networks are status games, and early "proof of work" earns outsized social capital. The mechanism under the tactics.

title: Don't End The Week With Nothing
note: Structure each week to finish owning a portable, compounding asset (a shipped artifact, a public reputation, a narrative you control) instead of an even hour-for-pay swap your employer keeps. The career-capital half of this section's title, made operational: prefer visible work, build reputation outside the employer, ship things you own.

title: Work with the garage door up
note: The person who coined the phrase on what building in public actually means: expose half-finished process and open problems, not polished launch posts, because the in-progress work is what builds an invested following and surfaces collaborators. Four minutes that reframe it from marketing toward thinking.
